988.title: kirtan repertoire (20 songs)
988.hook: a line sung back slower than it went out, and the old hymn that bows to the potter and the carpenter
988.howItsDone: At a kirtan, om namah shivaya is sung as a simple call-and-response line, often slowing over many rounds; Shaiva Hindus also repeat it as a mantra in daily japa.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kirtan repertoire: the first song of the night, to Ganesha, clearing the road. Did you name an obstacle before you began something? Day nine hundred eighty-eight.

The leader sings it quickly the first time, almost spoken. Om namah shivaya. The room sends it back a little slower. The leader slows to meet them. After a while nobody is rushing, and the line has stretched out like a rope being let down a well. There's no verse to remember, no chorus, no bridge. Just those few syllables, over and over, while the drum keeps time underneath. It's a simple song to learn. Its words, though, reach back into one of the old Vedic hymns.
screen: `SUNG FAST, SENT BACK SLOW.` → `NO VERSE, NO CHORUS.` → `A LINE FROM AN OLD HYMN.`

segments.voice: Om namah shivaya. Namah is a bow, a salutation: I bow, honor to. Shivaya is to Shiva, a name that also carries the sense of the kind one, the auspicious one. Put together: Om, I bow to Shiva. The words namah shivaya appear in the Shri Rudram, a long hymn to Rudra, the fierce form of Shiva, in the Krishna Yajur Veda. There they come in a line that bows to him twice over: to the kind one, and to the one who is kinder still, both names for the same Rudra. But the setting around that line is the surprise. The Rudram bows over and over, and it bows to Shiva in places you wouldn't expect. In the hunter, in the potter, in the carpenter, the chariot maker. In the forest, in the field, in the flowing water. In some lines it even names the lord of thieves. The hymn seems determined not to leave anything out. So the little kirtan line arrives carrying a whole world with it. When a group sings om namah shivaya, they're singing a phrase that once sat in a hymn bowing to every corner of life. That's worth knowing when the line comes round yet again. Repetition here isn't the same thing said again. Each time the room sends it back, it can be a bow to something different: the person beside you, the tired body, the noise from the street, the thing you don't want to face. Shaivas, the Hindus who worship Shiva as the highest, hold this mantra very close. But people from other Hindu homes sing it at kirtan too, and a newcomer can join in by the second round.
screen: `NAMAH: I BOW. SHIVAYA: TO SHIVA.` · `THE WORDS COME FROM THE RUDRAM.` · `THE HYMN BOWS TO EVERYONE.` · `EACH ROUND, A DIFFERENT BOW.` · then, large: `OM NAMAH SHIVAYA.`

segments.voice: Let the hands rest and the jaw loosen. On the out-breath, say the line silently, or aloud if you're alone: om namah shivaya. Each time it comes round, let it be a bow to one thing nearby. The chair holding you. The sound in the next room. Your own hands. Someone you'll see later today. If you pray, let the line be your prayer. If not, let it simply be a way of noticing, one thing at a time. The bell holds the time.
Kirtan repertoire. Today's song: om namah shivaya, I bow to Shiva, a line that comes from a hymn that bows to everything.
Your line: kirtan repertoire, twenty songs. Today, choose one ordinary worker you pass, a driver, a cook, a cleaner, and give them a small silent bow. Day nine hundred eighty-eight.

989.title: kirtan repertoire (20 songs)
989.hook: a lamp set on the doorstep lights the room and the street at once, and Tulsidas says the tongue is that doorstep
989.howItsDone: At kirtan, Shri Ram jai Ram jai jai Ram is sung back and forth, sometimes for a long stretch without changing a word; some Hindus also repeat Rama's name quietly through the day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kirtan repertoire: om namah shivaya, a line from a hymn that bows to the potter and the carpenter. Who got your silent bow? Day nine hundred eighty-nine.
screen: `KIRTAN REPERTOIRE.` · `OM NAMAH SHIVAYA, A BOW TO EVERYONE.`

segments.voice: One small clay lamp, and evening coming on. Put it inside, and the house is lit but the path outside is dark. Put it out in the lane, and the house goes black. Or set it right on the threshold, the step of the open door, where its light falls both ways at once. Tulsidas, the poet who retold the Ramayana in the language of ordinary people, takes that small household choice and turns it into a teaching about a name. Today's song is that name, Rama's.
screen: `ONE LAMP, ONE CHOICE.` → `INSIDE, OUTSIDE, OR THE DOORSTEP.` → `TODAY'S SONG: RAMA'S NAME.`

segments.voice: Shri Ram, jai Ram, jai jai Ram. Honor to Rama, victory to Rama, victory, victory to Rama. At a kirtan it goes back and forth like a rocking boat. Some groups sing it for a long time without changing a word. Why would anyone want only the name, over and over? Near the start of the Ramcharitmanas, Tulsidas stops the story before it begins and spends a long stretch praising Rama's name. In one couplet he gives the lamp picture. In paraphrase: set the jewel-lamp of Rama's name on the threshold of your tongue, if you want light both inside and outside. The tongue is the doorway between the self and the world. A name kept there lights both. Inside, the mind steadies. Outside, the words that leave your mouth come out a little different. Then Tulsidas pushes further, and this is the part that can startle. He argues that, in a way, the name is greater than Rama himself. Rama, in the story, came in person and helped those he met. The name, Tulsidas says, has gone on helping countless people who never met him at all. A king can only be in one kingdom. A name can be on every doorstep. Ideas like this stand behind nama-kirtan, the singing of the name. In Tulsidas's picture, the name needs only a tongue to rest on, and anyone can say it, anywhere. That's why the song is so plain. The plainness is the point.
screen: `SHRI RAM, JAI RAM, JAI JAI RAM.` · `A LAMP ON THE TONGUE'S DOORSTEP.` · `LIGHT INSIDE AND OUTSIDE.` · `THE NAME REACHES WHERE RAMA DIDN'T.` · then, large: `THE PLAINNESS IS THE POINT.`

segments.voice: Let the mouth relax, lips just touching. Rest your attention on the tongue, lying quiet behind the teeth. That's the doorstep. If you pray, you can set Rama's name there, saying it silently: Ram. Ram. Let it sit in the doorway and see whether it lights anything, inside or out. If you'd rather not use the name, rest your attention on that doorway anyway, and notice what wants to come out of it today. The bell holds the time.
Kirtan repertoire. Today's song: Shri Ram, jai Ram, jai jai Ram, Rama's name set like a lamp on the doorstep of the tongue.
Your line: kirtan repertoire, twenty songs. Today, before one hard conversation, pause at the doorstep of your tongue and choose what you set there. Day nine hundred eighty-nine.

990.title: kirtan repertoire (20 songs)
990.hook: a song that is nothing but a string of names, and the Gita verse where the word for singing God's glory turns up
990.howItsDone: Krishna devotees sing Govinda jaya jaya and similar strings of names at kirtans and in homes, often speeding up toward a clapping peak and slowing again to a hush.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kirtan repertoire: Rama's name, a lamp set on the doorstep of the tongue. Before a hard conversation, what did you set there? Day nine hundred ninety.

Govinda jaya jaya, Gopala jaya jaya. Radha Ramana Hari, Govinda jaya jaya. Read it on paper and it barely looks like a song. No story, no request, no rhyme to speak of. Just names, and the word jaya, victory, hung between them like lanterns on a wire. A kirtan can ride that line up to a fast, clapping peak and then let it fall back to a whisper. Someone hearing it for the first time might ask where the meaning is. The answer is in the names themselves, and in one verse of the Bhagavad Gita.
screen: `GOVINDA JAYA JAYA.` → `NAMES LIKE LANTERNS ON A WIRE.` → `WHERE IS THE MEANING?`

segments.voice: Each name in the song is a small portrait of Krishna. Govinda and Gopala both belong to the cowherd years in Vraja, the boy among the cows and the herders. Hari is a name of Vishnu, and devotees honor Krishna as one with Vishnu. Radha Ramana is the one who delights Radha, so the song quietly brings her into the room too. String the names together and you've told a story without telling it. Anyone who knows the stories hears them pass by. Now the Gita. In chapter nine, Krishna describes the great-souled ones who turn to him. In paraphrase: always singing my glory, striving, firm in their vows, bowing to me with devotion, they worship me, ever joined. The word there for singing his glory is kirtayantah, and you can hear kirtan in it. So the practice the room is doing has a place in the Gita itself. And it isn't presented as an extra for musical people. It's set alongside striving and keeping vows, as part of how the great-souled live. The Bhagavata Purana adds a voice from inside the practice. The sage Narada, who wanders the worlds with his vina, says that when he sings of the Lord's deeds, the Lord appears quickly in his heart, as if called. That's the hope a kirtan carries, quietly, every time a name goes out and comes back. Not that a song explains God. That a name, sung with attention, can work like a call. Which is why, for devotees, the song doesn't need more words. The names are already doing the calling.
screen: `EACH NAME, A SMALL PORTRAIT.` · `THE GITA: ALWAYS SINGING MY GLORY.` · `NARADA SINGS, AND THE LORD APPEARS.` · `A NAME SUNG WITH ATTENTION CALLS.` · then, large: `THE NAMES DO THE CALLING.`

segments.voice: Settle where you are. Bring to mind a few names you've called out in your life. A parent, a friend, a child, a pet at the door. Notice how each name carries a whole person with it, and how your voice changes for each one. Let them go. If you pray, you can take one name of God from your own tradition and say it silently, slowly, the way you'd call someone you hoped would come. If not, rest with the feeling of calling and being called. The bell holds the time.
Kirtan repertoire. Today's song: Govinda jaya jaya, a string of Krishna's names, each one a small portrait, sung like a call.
Your line: kirtan repertoire, twenty songs. Today, when you say someone's name, say it once with full attention, as if you were calling them, and notice their face. Day nine hundred ninety.

991.title: kirtan repertoire (20 songs)
991.hook: a refrain that never changes, and a list that slips in hunger, sleep and error beside peace and compassion
991.howItsDone: The ya devi sarva-bhuteshu verses are recited and sung in Goddess worship, especially during Navaratri, and at kirtans the room often joins the unchanging bow while a leader sings the changing word.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kirtan repertoire: Govinda jaya jaya, Krishna's names sung like a call. Whose name did you say with full attention? Day nine hundred ninety-one.
screen: `KIRTAN REPERTOIRE.` · `GOVINDA JAYA JAYA, NAMES AS A CALL.`

segments.voice: Halfway through the evening, the music changes key and the room turns toward the Goddess. The leader begins a verse that has the same ending every time, a run of bows that the whole room picks up almost at once. Only one word in the middle changes. Peace. Faith. Compassion. Mother. Words that sound right for a hymn to a goddess. But if you stay for the whole list, other words come round too, words nobody would put on a greeting card. Hunger. Sleep. Thirst. And, near the end, error.
screen: `THE ROOM TURNS TO THE GODDESS.` → `ONE WORD CHANGES EACH TIME.` → `PEACE, FAITH ... HUNGER, ERROR.`

segments.voice: The song comes from the Devi Mahatmya, the Glory of the Goddess, a text set inside the Markandeya Purana. In its fifth chapter the gods, driven from heaven, go to the Himalaya and praise her. The verse they repeat goes like this in Sanskrit: ya devi sarva-bhuteshu, and then a quality, rupena samsthita, namas tasyai, namas tasyai, namas tasyai, namo namah. In paraphrase: to the Goddess who dwells in all beings in the form of this, bow to her, bow to her, bow to her, bow, bow. Then the gods fill in the blank, verse after verse. Consciousness. Intelligence. Sleep. Hunger. Shadow. Power. Thirst. Patience. Modesty. Peace. Faith. Loveliness. Fortune. Memory. Compassion. Contentment. Mother. And error, the word bhranti, confusion, mistaking one thing for another. So the hymn doesn't only find her in the parts of life that look holy. It finds her in the tired body asking for sleep, the stomach asking for food, even the mind that gets things wrong. For Shaktas, Hindus who honor the Goddess as the highest, this is close to the heart of the matter: she is the power moving through everything, the plain and the bright alike. Sung as kirtan, the structure does something lovely. The bow at the end never changes, so even someone who doesn't know Sanskrit can join it from the second verse. The changing word is the leader's job. The room's job is to keep bowing, whatever word comes up. Hunger, bow. Error, bow.
screen: `FROM THE DEVI MAHATMYA.` · `TO THE GODDESS IN ALL BEINGS.` · `IN SLEEP, HUNGER, EVEN ERROR.` · `THE BOW NEVER CHANGES.` · then, large: `WHATEVER COMES UP, BOW.`

segments.voice: Check in with the body, from the stomach up. Is there hunger, tiredness, thirst, restlessness? Name whatever is here, plainly, one word at a time. Then name something brighter that's also here: a little patience, a memory, some contentment. Don't rank them. Let each word come and go like the changing word in the hymn. If you pray, you can follow each word with the hymn's refrain, said silently. If not, simply notice that both kinds of word belong to the same life. The bell holds the time.
Kirtan repertoire. Today's song: ya devi sarva-bhuteshu, to the Goddess in all beings, found in peace and compassion, and in hunger, sleep and error too.

Your line: kirtan repertoire, twenty songs. Today, the next time you catch yourself in a mistake, name it plainly once, the way the hymn names error, before any scolding starts. Day nine hundred ninety-one.

992.title: kirtan repertoire (20 songs)
992.hook: the music stops, a flame is lit on a plate, and everyone reaches toward it with both hands
992.howItsDone: Aarti often closes a puja or a kirtan: a lamp is waved before the deity while the group sings, then carried round so each person can pass their hands over the flame and touch their eyes and head.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kirtan repertoire: the Goddess in all beings, in peace and compassion, and in hunger, sleep and error too. Did you name a mistake plainly before the scolding started? Day nine hundred ninety-two.

Late in the evening the drum goes quiet. Someone lights a small flame on a brass plate, a wick in ghee or a piece of camphor, and stands before the image at the front of the room. The plate begins to move in slow circles. A bell rings in the other hand. The room stands and starts a song that some of them clearly know by heart. When the circling stops, the plate is carried through the room. People reach out with both hands, pass their palms over the flame, and draw the warmth back over their eyes and the top of the head.
screen: `THE DRUM GOES QUIET.` → `A FLAME ON A BRASS PLATE.` → `HANDS OVER THE FLAME, TO THE EYES.`

segments.voice: That's aarti: light waved before the deity, often as the closing act of a puja or a kirtan. The song sung with it is also called an aarti, and one of the aartis sung in Hindi is Om jai jagdish hare. Tradition credits the words to a Punjabi writer, Shardha Ram Phillauri. The opening, in paraphrase: Om, victory to you, Lord of the world, Hari, who removes in a moment the troubles of your devotees. Later comes a line that's easy to sing and hard to forget: you are my mother and my father; with whom else would I take shelter? Notice where the evening has gone. It began with Ganesha, clearing the road. Then Shiva, a bow to everything. Then Rama's name, a lamp on the tongue. Then Krishna's names, sung as a call. Then the Goddess, found even in hunger and error. And now the light itself is carried round, and people take it into their hands. A kirtan repertoire isn't just a playlist. It's a shape. It moves from beginning, through bowing and naming and calling, to receiving. One way to read the gesture at the end: the light that was offered up comes back to each person in the room. Families differ on the details, which aarti, which lamp, how many circles, and none of that needs settling here. In this telling of the evening, the turn is the point. The songs go out, the light comes back.
screen: `AARTI: LIGHT WAVED, A SONG SUNG.` · `YOU ARE MY MOTHER AND MY FATHER.` · `A REPERTOIRE HAS A SHAPE.` · `THE LIGHT COMES BACK TO EACH PERSON.` · then, large: `THE SONGS GO OUT. THE LIGHT COMES BACK.`

segments.voice: If there's a candle or a lamp nearby, you can light it, safely. If not, any light will do: a window, a screen dimmed low. Hold your hands up toward it, palms out, and feel whatever warmth or brightness reaches them. Then slowly bring the palms back and rest them over your closed eyes for a moment. If you pray, let this be your aarti. If not, let it simply be a moment of receiving something you didn't make. The bell holds the time.
Kirtan repertoire. The songs a group knows by heart, and the shape they make: from Ganesha at the start to the aarti, the light carried round at the end.

Your line: kirtan repertoire, twenty songs. Today, end one thing well: a meal, a call, a workday. Before moving on, take a breath that marks it finished. Tomorrow, a new road: jnana, the way of knowing. Day nine hundred ninety-two.

993.title: jnana: Shankara's *Vivekachudamani* (selections)
993.hook: a book about knowing that warns, early on, that clever talk about scripture sets nobody free
993.howItsDone: Some students of Advaita Vedanta read the Vivekachudamani slowly with a teacher, a few verses at a time, alongside periods of quiet reflection on what the verses point to.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last of our kirtan repertoire: the aarti, the light carried round and taken into each person's hands. What did you end well? Today the singing goes quiet, and a book opens. Day nine hundred ninety-three.
screen: `KIRTAN REPERTOIRE.` · `THE LIGHT COMES BACK.` · `NOW, A BOOK.`

segments.voice: Here is a strange thing for a book of philosophy to say about itself. Loud speech, a flood of words, skill in explaining the scriptures, deep learning: these, it says, give the learned a kind of enjoyment, but they don't set anyone free. That warning sits early in the Vivekachudamani, a teaching poem in Sanskrit that tradition credits to Shankara, the teacher of Advaita, non-duality. A book full of careful argument, telling its readers not to mistake careful argument for the goal. So what is the goal? The book has a word for it, and the word is today's: jnana.
screen: `A BOOK THAT WARNS ITS READERS.` → `LEARNING ISN'T FREEDOM.` → `SO WHAT IS JNANA?`

segments.voice: The name Vivekachudamani can be put into English as something like the crest-jewel of discernment, the gem worn at the very top. Viveka is discernment, telling the lasting from the passing. Jnana is knowing. But the book means a particular kind of knowing. Not knowing about something, the way you can know the capital of a country you've never seen. Knowing the way you know you're awake right now. Direct, first-hand, not borrowed. Early on, the book says three things are hard to come by, and come only by grace: a human birth, the longing to be free, and the shelter of a great soul, a real teacher. Then, before teaching anything, it clears the ground. People may quote scriptures, perform rites, worship the gods, it says, but without realizing the oneness of the Self, there is no freedom. And then a line that sounds almost like a riddle, in paraphrase: while the highest truth is unknown, study of scripture bears no fruit, and once it is known, study bears no fruit either. Some readers hear that as dismissive of books. It's closer to a map's honest word about itself. A map is priceless while you're lost and useless once you're home. Neither moment makes the map worthless. It only tells you what it's for. So when this path says jnana, it isn't praising the clever. On this reading, a grandmother who has never read a line of Sanskrit could know more, in this sense, than a professor who can recite the whole text. That's the knowing this book is after.
screen: `VIVEKA: DISCERNMENT. JNANA: KNOWING.` · `THREE THINGS HARD TO COME BY.` · `UNKNOWN OR KNOWN, STUDY ISN'T THE GOAL.` · `A MAP, PRICELESS UNTIL YOU'RE HOME.` · then, large: `KNOWING, NOT KNOWING ABOUT.`

segments.voice: For a few breaths, think about breathing: air in, air out, lungs, the word breath. Then let the thinking drop, and just feel one breath as it actually happens. The cool at the nostrils. The rise and fall. Notice the difference between the two. One is knowing about. The other is knowing. Go back and forth if it helps. If you pray, you can rest in that second kind of knowing as your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Jnana. Knowing, the direct kind, not knowing about. In the Vivekachudamani it's the knowing that frees, which no amount of clever talk can stand in for.
Your line: jnana, Shankara's Vivekachudamani, selections. Today, catch one moment when you're explaining something you haven't actually tried, and notice the gap. Day nine hundred ninety-three.

994.title: jnana: Shankara's *Vivekachudamani* (selections)
994.hook: what a student has to bring before the teaching begins, and the surprise word the list ends on
994.howItsDone: In Advaita teaching, the four qualifications, discernment, dispassion, the six treasures and the longing for freedom, are taught as preparation for the main texts, and students work on them as daily disciplines.

segments.voice: Yesterday, jnana: the direct kind of knowing, which clever talk can't replace. This week ran from the kirtan songs, Shiva, Rama, Govinda, the Goddess and the aarti, into a quiet book. Did you catch a gap between explaining something and trying it? Day nine hundred ninety-four.

What should a student bring to a teacher before the teaching even starts? A notebook, maybe. Some background reading. A good question. The Vivekachudamani has its own answer, and it's a list. Not of books or skills, but of inner qualities, set out one after another, like the things you'd pack before a long climb. Much of the list sounds stern: calm, restraint, endurance. Then, a little after the list ends, the text says which single thing matters most among all the means to freedom. For a book about knowing, the word it chooses is a surprise.
screen: `WHAT DO YOU BRING TO A TEACHER?` → `A LIST OF INNER QUALITIES.` → `AND ONE SURPRISE WORD.`

segments.voice: The Vivekachudamani names four things a seeker needs. First, viveka: discernment between the lasting and the passing. Second, vairagya: letting go of the hunger for enjoyments, here and in any heaven. Third, a group of six it calls treasures. Calm of mind. Restraint of the senses. Not leaning on outer things. Bearing hardship without complaint. Faith in the teaching and the teacher's words. And a mind that stays settled. Fourth, the longing to be free itself. Then the text says something practical. If dispassion and longing are strong, the calm and the rest bear fruit. If they're weak, the rest are like mirages in a desert, water that isn't there. So the engine of the whole list is wanting freedom, and being willing to let go. And then the surprise. In paraphrase: among all the means to freedom, bhakti, devotion, is the greatest. And bhakti, the text says, is the seeking of one's own true nature. That's worth a pause after a week of kirtan. The devotion of the singing room and the searching of the quiet book are not set against each other here. The book takes devotion's word and gives it its own meaning: to love the truth of who you are enough to keep looking for it. Read this way, the knower isn't asked to stop loving. The love is aimed at the search itself.
screen: `VIVEKA: THE LASTING FROM THE PASSING.` · `LETTING GO, AND SIX TREASURES.` · `THE LONGING TO BE FREE.` · `BHAKTI: SEEKING YOUR OWN NATURE.` · then, large: `LOVE AIMED AT THE SEARCH.`

segments.voice: Let the eyes close. Look over your day so far and sort it, gently, into two piles. Things that were passing: a mood, a headline, a craving, a small worry. And anything that seemed to stay. The book would point to the one who noticed all of it; see what you find. Don't argue with yourself about which pile something goes in. Just practice the sorting. That's viveka, in a small way. If you pray, you can hold the longing to know what lasts as your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Jnana. Knowing that frees. In the Vivekachudamani it rests on discernment, letting go, the six treasures and the longing to be free, and the text calls seeking your own nature bhakti.
Your line: jnana, Shankara's Vivekachudamani, selections. Today, when something grabs you, ask once: is this passing, or does it last? Day nine hundred ninety-four.
